### D793. sandbox-dev's limits for the hackathon's judging week: the relay's budgets up, the email budget sized to 30% of a shared SendGrid plan, named app shares and tighter per-IP limits
- Date 2026-11-13 · Status: **asked for by the user 2026-11-13** (raise the email and relay limits for the hackathon's judging week); the SendGrid plan and its sharing **stated by the user 2026-11-13**; values and the two overrides decided while building; **confirmed by the user 2026-11-13**; amended the same day after an independent security review (lows only: the run-time testnet gate, the alert count, `config_ignored`, the prefix day, the stamps app's 200) · Built: `envs/sandbox-dev.json` (`emailIssuer.dailySendBudget` 200 → 333, `emailIssuer.tighterLimits`; `near.relay`: `appDailyBudgetNear` 1 → 3, `dailyBudgetNear` 5 → 6, `activationsPerAppPerDay` 200 → 300, `lowBalanceNear` 2 → 9); `packages/env/src/email-issuer.ts` (`appShares`, `tighterLimits`, `EMAIL_APP_ID_RE`, `MAX_EMAIL_APP_SHARES`, their rules); `apps/email-issuer/scripts/gen-wrangler.ts` (`EMAIL_APP_SHARES`, `EMAIL_TIGHTER_LIMITS`); `apps/email-issuer/src/limits.ts` (`TighterLimits`, `parseTighterLimits`, `tighten`, `limitsFor(envName, tighter)`, `parseAppShares`, `namedAppShare`), `src/env.ts`, `src/handlers.ts` (`shareOf`, `appSharesOf`, `tighterLimitsOf`, `configIgnored`, `aggregateLimits`, the two `limitsFor` calls), `src/daily.ts` (`ALERT_KINDS`); tests `packages/env/src/email-issuer.test.ts`, `apps/email-issuer/scripts/test/gen-wrangler.test.ts`, `apps/email-issuer/scripts/test/sandbox-budget.test.ts`, `apps/email-issuer/test/env-overrides.test.ts`, `apps/api/scripts/test/near-relay-sandbox.test.ts`, `packages/core/test/integration-doc.test.ts` (unchanged, reads the manifest); docs `docs/operations.md` ("NEAR relay", the issuer's "Judging week on sandbox-dev", "Never past a free tier"), `docs/api.md`, `docs/integration.md` section 8's limits table, `docs/partner-start-here.md`, `docs/security.md`, `docs/system-overview.md`, `docs/mainnet-readiness.md` rows 1.21 and 4.9, `packages/playbooks/src/incidents.ts` (`near-relay-budget-high`, `near-relay-balance-low`) and the generated `docs/playbooks.md` · Number note: D792 is `chore/pre-public-tidy`'s
- Context: the repo goes public on 2026-11-14 and the hackathon's judges and the public use the hosted demo (Smoke B, plan `free`) and a new stamps demo app until about 2026-11-25. Google sign-in is closed to strangers (Testing mode: listed test users only, 100 in the project's lifetime, readiness 4.24), so email is their only way in. The SendGrid account the issuer, the admin Worker and the watchdog send through (one account, three keys, D414 as amended) is on **Essentials 50K** (the user, 2026-11-13): 50,000 mails a month, **shared with the user's other apps**: the account sent 1,342 in the 30 days to 2026-11-13 and about 6,300 in the 30 days before, all apps together (the user's SendGrid screenshot of 2026-11-13). SendGrid's public pages (read 2026-11-13) show no daily cap on paid plans, a monthly overage billed per mail on the next invoice (Twilio's overage table: $0.0013 a mail for Essentials 50K; its 2022 changelog: $19.95 a month), and, since 2026-06-25, sending stopped at 10 times the plan. So overage is billed, not refused: a cost the user hasn't approved (D417's spirit).
- Decision, email budget: `dailySendBudget` 333, the largest budget whose worst month stays within **30% of the 50,000-a-month plan**, the user's choice "to be safe" (2026-11-13) although the other apps' recent volume would leave room for half: `(budget + its 30% owner pool + 50 other mails a day) × 31` = 14,942 ≤ 15,000. The 50 is the issuer's own alerts (at most 25 a day: 5 kinds × `ALERT_MAILS_PER_KIND_PER_DAY` 5, which the test reads from the code) and about 25 for the admin Worker's notices and the watchdog's warnings and digest. **The 30% assumes critical watchdog alerts are acknowledged within the day**: one left open re-sends every 15 minutes (96 a day to sandbox-dev's one address), and a month with one open all month is 17,918 (35.8%); with the other apps' recent peak (about 6,300) beside it, about ten open at once would be needed to reach 50,000 (the test checks both). The other shares: 20% → 209, 50% → 582 (`sandbox-budget.test.ts` checks each is the largest that fits). The budget is the one value to change; the test's `ENV_SHARE` (0.3) holds the basis. What 333 gives: general pool 328 (the 80% line at 262), owner pool 99, Passport Home 19 + 13; a free-plan app 100 a day.
- Decision, the hackathon app's share: the per-app share (2% of the plan's `per_day`; `free` is the only plan and no command changes an app's plan, so a bigger plan would be a hand-written D1 row and update that also moves the app's login quotas) is the binding limit. A testnet-only `emailIssuer.appShares` (`{"app_…": mails}`, at most 8 apps, each at most the budget) gives a named app that share in place of its plan's, capped at the general pool, the 20% reserve still applying (tested); the Worker reads it only when `NEAR_NETWORK` is `testnet` (gen writes it from the manifest's network), so a hand-set var elsewhere is ignored; absent or malformed, every share is the plan's as before. Proposed for the stamps app once it exists: 200 (about 180 first sign-ins a day with resends at about one in ten; it leaves 128 of the 328 for the other apps and Passport Home, where 250 left 78; at least about 140 when the demo app and Passport Home are busy first). About 300 a day needs the 50% budget (582) with a share of 330: the user's call.
- Decision, abuse: a testnet-only `emailIssuer.tighterLimits` lowers the per-IP `start` window (sandbox-dev: 10 per 10 min, 30 a day; dev envs 30 and 300), `resend` (10 per 10 min; 30), code mails per address from one requester (5 per 15 min, 15 a day; 20 and 100) and the per-prefix `start` day (IPv4 /24, IPv6 /56 and /48: 100; 1000 in every env, so one /48 could otherwise fill the pool). The issuer applies each as the lower of it and the env's own limit, so it can't loosen anything and needs no network gate; absent or malformed, the env's set (D340) is unchanged. One IP can then cause at most 90 code mails a day (30 starts with up to 2 resends each), under a third of the general pool, one prefix at most 300: using up a day takes several addresses and prefixes. A room of judges behind one conference Wi-Fi address shares 30 sign-ins a day (10 per 10 minutes), a venue with several addresses in one /24 shares 100; IPv6 devices each have their own /64. Either override set but malformed (or the shares off testnet) logs one `config_ignored` warning per isolate with the var's name and reason, never its value.
- Decision, NEAR relay (sized for 200 new users a day doing about five writes each; measured on testnet 2026-11-13 by read-only RPC: an activation 0.007115 NEAR, a guestbook relay 0.000239, so a new user ≈ 0.0083 NEAR and 200 ≈ 1.7 NEAR a day): `appDailyBudgetNear` 3 (1 would stop at about 120 new users), `dailyBudgetNear` 6 (3 left for partners' apps), `activationsPerAppPerDay` 300 (300 × 0.0071 = 2.1 NEAR, inside 3), `lowBalanceNear` 9 (`inFlightNear` 3 + `dailyBudgetNear` 6: the hourly event and the System status tile turn amber with a full worst-case day still covered). Unchanged: `perSenderPerDay` 50, `perAppPerDay` 2000, `relaysPerDay` 10000, `relaysPerMinute` 200, `inFlightNear` 3, `maxGasTgas` 10, `activationsPerDay` 1000. The relay account must hold at least 3 + 9 + 6 = 18 NEAR, or with the low-balance line at 9 `near_relay_balance_low` fires every day; the top-up target is 25 (it held 9.985 on 2026-11-13). Every relay needs a signed-in user, so a stranger's spend through one app is bounded by its 3 NEAR a day (testnet NEAR).
- Put back on 2026-11-26 (after judging ends about 2026-11-25): the relay's four values to 1, 5, 200 and 2, `gen`, deploy the API; the email budget, `appShares` and `tighterLimits` reviewed with the user then.
- **Note, decided by the Tech Lead 2026-11-23** (the Tech Lead's answers of 2026-11-23 to the coordinator's five numbered questions: "1 yes, 2 leave, 3 yes, 4 yes, 5 leave"; recorded on branch `feat/demo-plain-wording-2`): the NEAR relay limits' put-back is **left for the December deploy of `next`**, not a separate small API deploy on 2026-11-26. Until then sandbox-dev keeps the judging-week values (3, 6, 300, 9). `docs/go-live-after-freeze.md` 1.1a puts the four values back on `next` (`appDailyBudgetNear` 1, `dailyBudgetNear` 5, `activationsPerAppPerDay` 200, `lowBalanceNear` 2) and phase 3 deploys them; its 0.9 and 5.3 say so. This also replaces D872 item 12's plan of an API-only deploy from the commit the API runs.
- Mainnet: production's SendGrid plan needs a monthly quota above all its mail together (31 × the issuer's 1.3 × `dailySendBudget`, the admin Worker's notices, the watchdog's alerts) with overage billing in mind (readiness 4.9); `appShares` and `tighterLimits` are testnet only (a production equivalent is a separate decision). The relay's mainnet limits stay row 1.21's decision.
- Rejected: a budget sized to the whole 50,000 (it is shared); a new D1 plan for the hackathon app (hand-written SQL on the live D1, no audit, and it moves the login quotas); raising the 2% constant or loosening the 80% reserve (every env); changing `DEV_LIMITS` in code (every `local*`/`sandbox*` env).
- Address impact: none.

## Passport stamps: the contract (branch `feat/stamps-contract`), 2026-11-13

Asked for by the user 2026-11-13 (a NEAR-only passport stamps demo for the hackathon). Three builds in parallel from
one shared interface: the contract D794–D797 (this branch), the site D798–D802, the art D803–D804. Current state:
`contracts/hana-stamps/README.md`, `docs/operations.md` "Hackathon demo stamps (NEAR)", `docs/security.md` "The
passport stamps demo contract".

### D794. The stamps contract: six stamps checked on chain, bounded per account, no owner, not payable
- Date 2026-11-13 · Status: **asked for by the user 2026-11-13 (a NEAR-only passport stamps demo for the hackathon); details decided while building, to confirm** · Built: `contracts/hana-stamps` (`src/lib.rs`, unit tests in `src/tests.rs`, `README.md`), near-sdk 5.24 like the guestbook, its own Cargo.lock and toolchain
- Confirmed by the user 2026-11-13.
- Decision: the shared interface's contract. `collect({stamp, note?, proof?})` for the predecessor, each of `arrival`, `sponsored` (signer ≠ predecessor), `own_fare` (signer = predecessor), `signature` (D795), `postcard` (a note of 1 to 140 Unicode scalar values after `str::trim`) and `layover` (≥ 120 000 ms of block time after `arrival`) at most once, `arrival` first. Views `get_passport({account_id}) → {account_id, stamps} | null` (stamps in the order collected), `recent({from_index?, limit?})` (a ring of the latest 100 `{account_id, stamp, block_timestamp_ms}`, newest first, `limit` defaults to and is clamped at 50, as the guestbook's), `totals() → {passports, stamps}`, `catalog()`. A stored stamp is `{stamp, block_timestamp_ms, sponsored, note?}`; `note` is absent from the JSON, not `null`, on every stamp but `postcard`. `new()` runs in the deploy transaction; no owner, admin method, upgrade or migration; not payable.
- Decided while building (the spec left them open): `collect` returns the stamp it stored (as the guestbook's `add_message` returns the message); a `note` on any stamp but `postcard` is `ERR_BAD_NOTE` and a `proof` on any stamp but `signature` `ERR_BAD_PROOF`, so nothing unchecked is ever stored; the panic message is exactly the code (`ERR_NO_ARRIVAL`, nothing after it), checked in a fixed order (unknown stamp, misplaced note or proof, already / no arrival, the stamp's rule; README "Rules"); `sponsored` is recorded on every stamp, not only on `sponsored`; storage is one `LookupMap<AccountId, Vec<StoredStamp>>` entry per passport with the stamp id as a one-byte borsh enum tag (catalog order), the ring a `Vector` like the guestbook's, and two counters.
- Storage and abuse: one account costs at most about 740 bytes (the six stamps and a 140-character note of four-byte characters; 124 bytes for an arrival alone, about 200 for a typical passport), the ring at most about 12 200 bytes; the number of passports isn't bounded. Through the relay a new passport needs a new Journear user (`requireKnownAccount`) and each relay adds at most one, so sandbox-dev's limits bound the growth at about 15 NEAR a day through one app (`perAppPerDay` 2 000) and 74 across the environment (`relaysPerDay` 10 000) in the worst case; directly, an attacker pays about as much as the contract stakes. When the balance is used up new stamps fail and a transfer tops it up; recommended balance 10 NEAR, watched during the judging.
- Why: the contract is the only party the demo needs to trust, so every rule is its own; bounded per account because the caller has no NEAR to pay for storage; the stable codes let the site map each failure.
- Rejected: a cap on the number of passports (another error the site would have to handle; a full contract fails the same way an empty balance does, and testnet NEAR is free); storing stamp ids as strings (5–10 more bytes a stamp); accepting a note on other stamps and ignoring it.
- Address impact: none (no path, key or derivation input changes).

### D795. The signature stamp verifies the vault's NEP-413 signature on chain, pinned by a cross-language vector
- Date 2026-11-13 · Status: as D794 · Built: `contracts/hana-stamps/src/lib.rs` (`nep413_bytes`, `implicit_public_key`, `proof_is_valid`), `contracts/hana-stamps/tests/nep413-vector.json`, `packages/core/test/near-stamps-vector.test.ts`, the unit tests' `signature_*` cases, `contracts/integration-tests/tests/stamps.rs`, `apps/api/test-sandbox/stamps.test.ts`
- Confirmed by the user 2026-11-13.
- Decision: `proof = {message, nonce, recipient, signature}` as `hana.near.signMessage` takes and returns them; the contract rebuilds `u32le(2^31 + 413) ‖ borsh({message, nonce: [u8; 32], recipient, callback_url: None})`, hashes it with sha256 and checks it with `env::ed25519_verify` against the caller's implicit account id as the key. `recipient` must be the contract's own account id and `message` exactly `"Stamp my passport: " + caller`. A named account is `ERR_NOT_IMPLICIT` with or without a proof; anything else wrong is `ERR_BAD_PROOF`. Nonce and signature: standard base64 with padding (what `@hana-id/core`'s `base64Encode` writes), of exactly 32 and 64 bytes, the length checked before decoding. The nonce is not tracked (the stamp is once per account); the proof is not stored. The site must not pass a `callbackUrl` (a signature with one doesn't verify).
- The vector: `@hana-id/core`'s `encodeNep413Message` + `signNep413Message` (the vault's own path) sign for two TEST keys derived from public labels (never funded, not in the file); the TypeScript test writes (`HANA_WRITE_STAMPS_VECTOR=1`) and pins the JSON, the Rust tests read it with `include_str!` and must accept A's and B's own proofs and refuse each altered field, another recipient, the contract on another account, A's message signed by B's key, A's proof from B, a callback URL, a named account, wrong lengths, unpadded and base64url encodings. The sandbox tests sign with an independent Rust encoder; the API's sandbox test signs with the SDK's signer and relays through the relay's own code to the deployed wasm.
- Why: the stamp's point is a signature checked on chain; binding message and recipient to the caller and the contract makes a proof useless to anyone else.
- Rejected: accepting a `publicKey` in the proof and checking it is an access key of the caller (a cross-contract view; implicit accounts make the key the account); tracking nonces (no replay to prevent); accepting a callback URL (one more field to check for nothing).
- Address impact: none.

### D796. `deploy-stamps` is `deploy-guestbook`'s code with the stamps contract's settings; tests in every lane
- Date 2026-11-13 · Status: as D794 · Built: `scripts/lib/demo-deploy.ts` (the shared flow), `scripts/lib/guestbook-deploy.ts` (now the guestbook's settings over it, same exports), `scripts/lib/stamps-deploy.ts`, `scripts/deploy-stamps.ts`, `scripts/test/stamps-deploy.test.ts` (and `test/guestbook-deploy.test.ts` unchanged and green); `scripts/verify.mjs` `CONTRACT_CRATES`, `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, `scripts/dep-audit.mjs` `CARGO_LOCKS`, `scripts/dep-audit-allow.json` (RUSTSEC-2026-0009 as for the guestbook: the same lockfile), their tests; `contracts/integration-tests/tests/common/meta.rs` (the guestbook test's meta-transaction helpers, moved to be shared), `tests/stamps.rs`, `common::stamps_wasm`; `apps/api/test-sandbox/sandbox.ts` (`signDelegate`, `relayTx` moved from `meta-tx.test.ts`, `stampsWasm`), `test-sandbox/stamps.test.ts`
- Confirmed by the user 2026-11-13.
- Decision: one implementation of D743's flow (dry run by default, deploy + `new()` in one transaction, never a redeploy, `--lock` deletes every key, the testnet and keychain checks), parameterised by the crate, the manifest field, the probe view (`total_messages` for the guestbook, `totals` for the stamps contract, which must answer `{"passports":0,"stamps":0}` after `new()`) and the balance to require (stamps: the code, 200 000 bytes of state and 0.1 NEAR, about 3.6 NEAR). The guestbook's outputs and exports are unchanged. The contract lane tests and builds `contracts/hana-stamps`; the sandbox lane runs `tests/stamps.rs` (the full passport through real delegate actions and a direct `own_fare`, the layover on the sandbox clock by fast-forward, every refusal, gas with the ring empty and full) and then the API's `test-sandbox/stamps.test.ts`.
- Gas measured (near-sandbox 2.13.4, each `collect` attaching 10 Tgas, sandbox-dev's `maxGasTgas`): the `collect` receipt burns 1.51 (`arrival`), 1.55 (`sponsored`), 1.84 (`signature`), 1.63 (`postcard`, 140 four-byte characters), 1.63 (`layover`), 1.63 (`own_fare`, direct) Tgas; 1.54 and 1.85 with the ring full; a whole relayed transaction 3.0 to 3.3 Tgas. Every stamp fits the cap; no manifest change.
- Rejected: a copy of `guestbook-deploy.ts` (two copies of the safety checks to keep in step).
- Not done by the build (the user runs it): the account's creation, the deploy, the API's `gen` and deploy for the new receiver, the lock (`docs/operations.md` "Hackathon demo stamps (NEAR)").
- Address impact: none.

- Date 2026-11-13 · Status: as D794 · Built: `packages/env/src/schema.ts` (`nearSchema`, `nearRules`, `nearRelayRules`), `packages/env/src/near.test.ts`, `src/index.test.ts`, `envs/sandbox-dev.json`, `envs/README.md`, `apps/api/test/near-relay.test.ts` (the second receiver), `docs/integration.md` and `docs/partner-start-here.md` (the allowlist sentence), `packages/core/test/integration-doc.test.ts`, `docs/operations.md`

### D800. One collector per stamp on the demo's relayed flow; availability computed on the page, the contract decides
- Date 2026-11-13 · Status: asked for by the user 2026-11-13 (a NEAR-only passport stamps demo for the hackathon); details decided while building, to confirm · Built: `apps/stamps/src/collector.ts`, `src/stamps.ts`, `src/view.ts`, `src/app.ts`, `test/collector.test.ts`, `test/stamps.test.ts`, `test/view.test.ts`, `test/app.test.ts`; `apps/e2e/tests/stamps.spec.ts`, `src/server/stamps-contract.ts`
- Confirmed by the user 2026-11-13.

The page decides what looks open (Arrival first, Own fare's balance, implicit accounts for Signature, the layover's countdown from the Arrival's block time plus 3 s); the contract's `ERR_*`, the vault's and the relay's refusals come back on the stamp in plain words. A collected stamp shows at once (optimistic), is inked once (`fresh` in one update) and is confirmed from the chain; `recent` is read as two pages (0 and 50, limit 50), whatever order the ring answers in. Chain data is parsed strictly and notes made safe as D753.

## Passport stamps demo: the UI (branch `feat/stamps-art`), 2026-11-13

### D803. The passport and its six stamps are drawn in code, from the brand's tokens: no image files
- Date 2026-11-13 · Status: **asked for by the user 2026-11-13** (a NEAR-only passport stamps demo for the hackathon); details decided while building, to confirm · Built: `apps/stamps/src/ui/art.ts`, `apps/stamps/src/ui.css`, the preview harness `apps/stamps/preview/`
- Confirmed by the user 2026-11-13.
- Decision: every picture on the stamps site is inline SVG built by `src/ui/art.ts` with `createElementNS`: the six stamps (round, cut-corner ticket, oval, shield, postmark with wavy lines, hexagon; each with its title on a curve or in a band, a glyph, and its date in UTC drawn from the stamp's `atMs`), their empty outlines, the relay's "no gas" chop, the recent list's small icons, the identity page's 5 × 5 portrait (a hash of the account id), the page guilloche, and the Journear mark from `@hana-id/brand`'s geometry (D789). The art sets no colour: strokes and fills are `currentColor`, and `ui.css` gives each stamp an ink from `--jp-*` tokens per scheme with `light-dark()` (teal, orange, info blue, deep teal, danger red, warning amber; lighter tokens on the dark page). The ink texture is one SVG filter per stamp (edge roughening and two noises turned into alpha), cheap to render; the "inked" press animation is CSS, played once per stamp when the view marks it `fresh`, never under reduced motion.
- Why: no image requests and no `data:` URIs for the page's CSP to allow, the art follows the light and dark schemes and the token values without a second set of files, and the date is part of the stamp rather than a caption beside it.
- Rejected: PNG or SVG files per stamp (a set per scheme, and the date can't be in them); web fonts or images for the ink texture (requests, licences).
- Address impact: none.

- Date 2026-11-13 · Status: decided while building, to confirm · Built: `apps/stamps/src/ui/index.ts`, `text.ts`, `types.ts`, tests in `apps/stamps/test/ui/`
- Confirmed by the user 2026-11-13.
- Decision: (1) the UI module is safe on its own even though the site passes chain data through already neutralised (D753): every view string goes into a text node after the same replacement the demo uses (controls, bidi and invisible format characters become U+FFFD, a zero-width joiner between two pictographs kept), the postcard's note sits in a `dir="auto"` element with `unicode-bidi: isolate`, no view string becomes an attribute, and a link is kept only when it resolves to http(s) without credentials (another origin opens in a new tab with `rel="noopener noreferrer"`). (2) `PassportView` gains an optional `shareUrl` (the public passport's link, shown shortened on the identity page); left out, the line isn't shown. (3) In public mode a slot that isn't collected is drawn as an empty, locked slot with no control, whatever status the view gives it ("Not collected yet" unless the view gives a locked reason). The postcard's `collect` call passes the field's text trimmed, at most 140 Unicode scalar values (the contract's count; the field's `maxlength` of 140 UTF-16 units is never looser).

### D807. The stamps site's hand-check fixes: Signature's two approvals in one window with a Continue fallback; Own fare's faucet in the slot, one that takes implicit accounts
- Date 2026-11-13 · Status: found by the user's hand check 2026-11-13 (three findings: the Signature stamp's second
  approval needed the SDK's launcher; the faucet link was nowhere to be seen; the faucet refused the account), details
  decided while building, to confirm · Built: `apps/stamps/src/{collector,app,view,config}.ts`, `src/ui/`, `src/ui.css`,
  `apps/e2e/tests/stamps.spec.ts`.
- Confirmed by the user 2026-11-13.
- Cause (Signature): the second request (`signDelegateAction` with the proof) is made after awaits (the vault signs the
  NEP-413 message; the page then read NEAR when its read was older than 60 s; the vault checks the delegate's key on
  both RPC providers before it queues it, about 3.3 s on `rpc.testnet.near.org` today). It can only land in the window
  still open from the first approval (the window waits 15 s for a follow-up after an answer and says "You can go back
  to Stamp Trail", with Close now). Once that window is gone (closed by the user, timed out), the page has no user
  activation left (`packages/web/src/client/approval-window.ts` `prepare()`: no activation, no window) and the vault
  shows its "Review in Journear Passport" launcher (`packages/web/src/vault/approvals.ts` `pump()`/`syncLauncher()`).
- Decision: (1) The page awaits nothing between the two: the read the second request needs starts in the click (not
  awaited, so the first signing call is still made in it) and runs while the user approves the first; the second is
  sent the moment the first resolves. (2) The signed proof is kept in memory for the page session (cleared on success,
  a contract refusal, a relay that sent it, sign-out): a later click sends only the second request. (3) The slot shows
  a new UI state, `continue` (`{ stage, action }`): "Step 2 of 2: send your signed message to the contract." with
  **Continue** when the second approval waits on the launcher (its click calls `hana.prepareApproval()`, which opens
  the window the vault adopts for the waiting request) or was declined or closed (its click sends the second request
  from the click). Any other stamp whose approval waits on the launcher shows the same button ("Your approval is
  ready. Continue opens it in the Journear Passport window."). (4) Copy: the blurb "Two approvals: sign a message, then
  send it. The contract checks it on chain."; stages "Approval 1 of 2: sign the message…", "Approval 2 of 2: send it to
  the contract…".
- Decision (Own fare): the locked slot carries its own help (`detail`, `href`/`hrefLabel`, `copyAccount` on the UI's
  locked state): "The one stamp that needs your own testnet NEAR", "Copy your account id, paste it into NEAR’s faucet
  (free, no sign-up), then come back: this unlocks when the NEAR arrives.", **Get testnet NEAR ↗**, **Copy account id**
  (the full 64-hex id); "Get testnet NEAR ↗" also beside the balance. The faucet is NEAR's docs faucet
  (`https://docs.near.org/getting-started/faucet`): its page accepts `^[a-z0-9]+(?:[._-][a-z0-9]+)*$`, 2 to 64
  characters, creates a throwaway `docs-<hex>.testnet` account through `helper.testnet.near.org`, sends 5 NEAR to the id
  given and deletes the throwaway (checked on chain 2026-11-13: a 5 NEAR transfer to a 64-hex account). near-faucet.io,
  linked before, accepts only `*.testnet` names and `0x` addresses in its page, so every Journear Passport account was
  refused. While Own fare is locked for want of NEAR, the balance is read every 5 s while the tab is visible and at once
  when the window regains focus.
- Not changed: the SDK and the vault (no auto-approval, no skipped confirmation, nothing a ticket allows widened).
- Rejected: a Journear "starter NEAR" drip, for now (the relay's `activationYocto` can send up to 0.01 NEAR to new
  accounts by manifest, but it shares the sponsored-relay budget and reaches no existing account; a once-per-user drip
  is a new API route, about a day's work): the Tech Lead's call after the deadline.
- Possible later (SDK/vault): the approval window could say "One more approval is coming…" (and hold its idle close)
  while the vault prepares a follow-up from the same page, instead of "You can go back to Stamp Trail"; or a request
  flag letting the page say the next request is a follow-up.
- Address impact: none.

## The approval window in plain words (branch `feat/approval-plain-summary`), 2026-11-17

The Tech Lead's decision after stakeholder feedback: Journear Passport's users aren't Web3 users, and an approval window
that decodes or shows a transaction's raw payload confuses them. Current state: `docs/architecture.md` "Signing:
approval popup vs auto-approve", `docs/security.md` "Browser (`packages/web`)".

### D808. Design A: a plain summary at the top of every approval; the technical details behind "Show details", which the user can always open
- Date 2026-11-17 · Status: **decided by the user 2026-11-17** (Design A); the layout's details **confirmed by the user
  2026-11-17** (with D810 amended) · Built on `feat/approval-plain-summary` (from `next`), not merged, not deployed:
  `packages/core/src/decode/summary.ts` (`summarizeApproval`), `packages/web/src/auth/render-approval.ts`
  (`renderApproval`, `detailsSection`, `DETAILS_LABELS`), `auth/approve-page.ts`, `auth/css/approval.css`; tests
  `packages/core/test/approval-summary.test.ts`, `packages/web/test/auth/approval-summary.test.ts`,
  `apps/e2e/tests/approval-summary.spec.ts`.
- Decision: every approval starts with one plain headline ("{App} wants to send 0.1 NEAR to bob.testnet", "{App} wants
  to use stamps.testnet (collect)", "{App} wants you to sign a message for {recipient}"), a few plain lines, and two facts:
  the network and the most the network fee can be ("Network fee: up to 0.0001 ETH"; for a relayed NEAR action "paid
  for you by a relayer, not from your account"). The technical details (nonce, sequence, block and transaction hashes,
  gas limit and per-gas prices, access list, ledger footprint, the Stellar passphrase string, validity windows, the raw
  arguments of a call the summary already names, the field-by-field operation and action lists, the Support ID and its
  hint, a summarised typed-data tree) are in a native `<details>` the user opens with "Show details" (the label reads
  "Hide details" while open). The details always start folded, for every request (D810 as amended by the user). No
  partner setting: a partner setting that starts the details open may come later, and
  nothing a partner controls may ever reduce what a user can see.
- Why: the Tech Lead's audience; the facts a user decides on stay in view, the rest is one click away for those who
  want it.
- Not changed: what is decoded, what the vault checks and signs, the approval digest, the Approve guard (D36, D113:
  opening or closing the details neither arms nor resets it, a test checks), auto-approve.
- Address impact: none.

### D809. Every warning is always visible, never folded, never hideable
- Date 2026-11-17 · Status: **decided by the user 2026-11-17**; the list below **confirmed by the user 2026-11-17** ·
  Built: as D808.
- Decision: outside the fold, always, the red banners and lines first, right under the headline (nothing a partner
  sizes, such as the number of operations, can push them down; amended after the security review of 2026-11-17): the
  app's name, logo and origin; the account line; recipient and amount
  ("Sends", "NEAR leaving your account"); the network fee line; every red banner and danger line that exists
  (Stellar and NEAR account control with each operation's or action's own line, now above the details while the
  operation keeps its red frame inside them; a call to a contract on the user's own account; a global contract's burn;
  raw signing; D48, D52, D110, D723); the new spend warnings (D811); the "Journear can't explain" line (D810); a
  NEP-413 recipient with its mismatch and look-alike lines; the network as checked or "as the app says" (D726) and
  "isn't tied to one network" or "one chain" (D35; typed data's line reworded "This signature isn’t tied to one chain:
  it may be valid on any of them."); the test-app note and the whole mainnet demo block (D428, D492); the contract next
  to any function name; the overflow note on any box in view; the out-of-policy reason. Also kept in view, decided
  while building: a Stellar memo (an exchange tells deposits apart by it, so a changed memo can credit someone else),
  a signed message's text, who pays a fee-bump's fee (a summary line), an extra-preconditions warning, the NEAR relayer
  and network notes. Steps that move or grant value or change who controls the account (payments, path payments,
  offers, claimable balances and claiming them, merges, pool operations, contract calls, token transfers and
  approvals, trust lines, sponsorships begun or revoked; every NEAR action but account creation: transfers, every
  function call (one with no deposit can still move tokens held in that contract), key, stake and contract changes)
  are listed first. Since D814 (the Tech Lead's decision after seeing the 100-step screen) the steps are grouped in at
  most four lines, with a red or amber line for any left out; the numbered list (up to 20 value steps, then five
  others) it replaced is history. A
  Stellar transaction with such steps on the user's account says "XLM leaving your account: up to N" (payments,
  account creation, a path payment's most paid, offers selling XLM, a buy offer's most paid, claimable balances;
  "all of it" for a merge; contract calls and pool deposits can take more, which it says), as NEAR's total does.
  Anything left out of the list makes the request not explainable (D810) and says so (amended after the second
  security review of 2026-11-17). Colours of the risk lines: red where the unreadable part could move value or
  control with no visible bound, amber otherwise (D810).
- Address impact: none.

### D810. A request Journear can't explain states its risk in plain words; the details always start folded
- Date 2026-11-17 · Status: **decided by the user 2026-11-17**, **amended by the user 2026-11-17** (the details always
  start folded, raw signing included; first built as "open when Journear can't explain, never foldable for raw
  signing"), confirmed with that amendment · Built: `summarizeApproval`'s `explainable`, `cannotTell`,
  `stepsNotListed`, the `raw_signing` line; `render-approval.ts` `detailsSection`.
- The Tech Lead's reasoning, in their words: "if we open automatically when we can't explain the request in plain words
  or it's too many steps or raw signing, what makes you think that the user knows what they're looking at? I think
  it's better to hide and then clearly state the risks. If we just expand and show everything it makes the user even
  more confused."
- Decision: the technical details always start folded, in every case, and the user can always open them ("Show
  details"). Every case that used to open them carries a plain risk line above the fold instead, standing on its own
  (texts reworded under D853 on 2026-11-18, branch `feat/plain-approval-wording`: one shape, "Journear can’t check
  what this does[ (why)]. {the risk} {ending}", red ending "If you’re not sure, reject it.", amber ending "Approve only
  if you expected this from {App}."; "Technical details are below" is no longer said as advice, the details stay one
  tap away):
  - can't explain: "Journear can’t check what this does[ (why)]. It could take your money or tokens. If you’re not
    sure, reject it." (red), or the same with the amber ending;
  - a message that isn't text: "Journear can’t check what this does (the message isn’t readable text). Approve only if
    you expected this from {App}." (amber; since D886's note of 2026-11-23 "Journear can’t read this message, so it’s
    shown below in its raw form. Approve only if you expected this from {App}.", "Superseded or amended");
  - steps left out (D814): "Journear can’t check everything this does (it does N things at once and not all are
    listed here). Approve only if you expected this from {App}." (amber), or, when a left-out step moves or grants
    value or changes control, "… Some of the steps left out move money or tokens, or change who controls your
    account. If you’re not sure, reject it." (red);
  - raw signing: headline "{App} wants you to sign something Journear can’t read", line "Signing this could hand over
    your whole account and everything in it. Reject it unless you know exactly why you’re signing." (red; it replaces
    the older raw line in the window);
  - in the same family (reworded under D853): a malformed NEAR token call "Journear can’t check what this does (it
    uses {method} on {contract} in a non-standard way). …" (red); typed data that calls itself Permit2 for another
    contract "Journear can’t check what this does. It says it’s Permit2, a well-known way to let others take your
    tokens, but it isn’t the real one. It may be a scam. Reject it unless you know exactly why {App} needs it." (red;
    it keeps its own advice, after the review of PR 80); a possible permit
    "Journear can’t check what this does (it may be a permission for someone else to take your tokens). Approve only
    if you expected this from {App}." (amber); the internal fallback "Journear can’t check what this does (it couldn’t
    read this request). It could take your money or tokens. If you’re not sure, reject it." (red);
  - an unreadable offer price, a pool deposit or withdrawal, a Soroban call's extra authorizations keep their own
    lines too.
- Colours: red where the unreadable part could move value or control with no visible bound (raw signing; an unknown
  contract call on EVM, NEAR or Soroban, with or without value; `multicall`; an ERC-1155 batch too long to list;
  unexplained typed data; a Soroban call or authorization entry with extra authorizations; a Soroban contract
  creation that holds any authorization or runs a constructor, every call it authorizes listed in its own line;
  left-out steps that move value); amber otherwise (contract creation on EVM, whose value is shown; Soroban creation
  with neither, or code upload; a pool operation, whose amounts are shown; a
  conditional claim; an unreadable offer price, whose amount is shown; a Permit2 witness transfer, whose spends are
  warned about; a message that isn't text; left-out steps that move nothing).
- Final review (2026-11-17): every early return in the summary was checked under the always-folded rule for a fact
  that only the opened details used to show and that is now neither listed nor warned in red. Fixed: a Soroban
  contract creation's authorizations (above), and a NEAR function-call key's fee allowance, now in its line ("…,
  spending up to 0.25 NEAR on fees", or "with no limit on the NEAR it spends on fees"). The rest keep a visible line or
  a red warning for anything that decides what the user gives up.
- Trade-off, the Tech Lead's: the technical facts are one tap away, not on screen, for exactly the requests Journear
  can't explain; the risk is stated in plain words instead.
- The rule (the security review of
  2026-11-17): when the summary can't carry every term that decides what the user gives up, the request is not
  explainable. Not explainable: an EVM call with
  an unknown selector, too-short data, a known selector whose arguments don't decode, `multicall`, and contract
  creation; typed data other than D811's permits; a message that isn't plain text (shown as hex); a Soroban call or
  authorization that isn't a SEP-41 token `transfer` or `approve` with exactly their argument types; any Soroban call
  or authorization entry whose authorizations hold anything besides exactly that call (same contract, function and
  arguments) with nothing under it, each such other call said in a line of its own ("It also authorizes sending …");
  contract creation or code upload on Stellar; a liquidity pool deposit or withdrawal (the request names the pool, not
  its two assets; its amounts are said); a claimable balance with a conditional claimant; an offer whose price isn't
  two positive integers (never divided by); a list of steps that leaves any out (D809); an ERC-1155 batch of more than
  five kinds of item; a NEAR function call whose arguments aren't strict JSON or whose method name can't be shown as text; raw.
  Explainable, each with its deciding terms in the summary: Stellar payments, account creation, path payments (the
  most paid, the least received), offers (the least a sell returns, the most a buy costs, at the offer's price, and
  which existing offer it changes), claimable balances (who can claim), trust lines and the rest of the classic
  operations (D110); a NEAR function call with JSON arguments ("use {contract} ({method})", the Tech Lead's example), its
  arguments folded (an accepted trade-off). The summary is total: if building it fails on any value the decoders let
  through, the request gets "{App} wants you to approve a request Journear can't explain" with a red "Journear
couldn’t read this request. Reject it unless you are certain.", not explainable (reworded under D853: "{App} wants you
to approve something Journear can’t read", with the red fallback line above). Every summary the unit, renderer and
e2e approval tests build is checked never to be that fallback, so the catch can't hide a bug.
- Amended 2026-11-17 (branch `feat/evm-sponsored-approval`, after an automated review; decided while building,
  **confirmed by the user 2026-11-18**): a NEAR call to a standard value-moving method (`ft_transfer`, `ft_transfer_call`, `nft_transfer`,
  `nft_transfer_call`, `nft_approve`) whose arguments aren't exactly the standard's shape (its keys and no others, an
  amount a canonical decimal string, account ids valid, a memo or message a string or null as the standard has it, an
  `approval_id` a u64) is no longer the plain "Use tok.testnet (ft_transfer)" line: the contract may read such arguments
  leniently and move tokens the summary didn't show (a parser differential). It reads "Use tok.testnet (ft_transfer)
  with arguments that don’t match the token standard", is not explainable, and gets a red line naming the method:
  "Journear can’t tell what this request does: it calls ft_transfer on tok.testnet with arguments that don’t match the
  token standard exactly. It could move your money or tokens. …" (it replaces the generic red line). Any other NEAR
  call with JSON arguments stays explainable, as decided above (it names the contract and the method), but one whose
  method name contains `transfer`, `withdraw`, `approve`, `send`, `swap`, `execute`, `burn`, `remove_liquidity`,
  `unwrap`, `claim`, `redeem` or `stake` (anywhere, so `storage_withdraw` and `unstake` too) or starts with `mt_` (the
  multi-token standard), and doesn't start with `get_`, `view_`, `is_` or `has_` (read calls), gets an amber line, code `may_move_tokens`: "This calls {method} on
  {contract}: a call like this may move tokens or NEAR you hold with that contract. Approve only if you expected it."
  (once per method and contract). Built: `summary.ts` (`NEAR_STANDARD_METHODS`, `nearStandardShape`,
  `NEAR_VALUE_METHOD`); tests in `approval-summary.test.ts` (each malformed shape, the pattern list, grouping and
  `shownSteps`) and `render-approval-sponsored.test.ts`.
- Why the NEAR/Soroban difference: a NEAR action carries the NEAR it moves in the action itself (the visible "NEAR
  leaving your account"), and its arguments are JSON the user can read when opened; a Soroban call's authorization tree
  can move tokens the summary can't weigh. **confirmed by the user 2026-11-18 (with D808–D813)**.
- Address impact: none.

### D811. Plain warnings for requests that let someone spend the user's tokens
- Date 2026-11-17 · Status: **decided by the user 2026-11-17**; the detection rules, thresholds and wording
  **confirmed by the user 2026-11-17** · Built: `summary.ts` (`spendWarning`, `PRACTICALLY_UNLIMITED`, `PERMIT2_ADDRESS`).
- Decision: "This lets {spender} spend up to {amount} …, until it is used up or you take the permission back." (amber),
  or, at or above the type's max ("with no limit") or with no practical limit, "This lets {spender} spend all of your
  {token}, …, until you take the permission back. Approve only if you trust it completely." (red). No practical limit
  (amended after the security review): 10^27 of the smallest units for a token Journear doesn't know (a billion whole
  tokens even at 18 decimals, below 2^96), more than a trillion whole tokens for a pinned one (more than its supply).
  Raw amounts carry thousands separators. A Soroban `approve` from another account says whose tokens, never "your". The spender
  is named when it is on Journear's verified-contracts list for that chain ("Sodax Asset Manager (0x…, verified by
  Journear)"), else shown as its address, "an address Journear hasn’t verified", or "(the zero address)". An amount of
  0 is a revoke: a plain headline ("take back … permission"), no warning, except an ERC-20/721 `approve(spender, 0)`
  on a contract not on the pinned list with a spender other than the zero address: ERC-721 shares the selector and
  item 0 exists, so it reads "change {spender}'s permission" with an amber line saying it may let them take item 0.
  Covered: ERC-20 `approve` (which ERC-721's `approve` shares: for a token Journear doesn't know, the warning adds "If
  the contract is an NFT collection, it lets them take your item {n} instead."), `increaseAllowance` ("a further"), `permit` sent as a transaction when the owner
  is the user; ERC-721/1155 `setApprovalForAll(true)` (red: every item, now and later); EIP-712 typed data, strictly:
  EIP-2612 `Permit` (exactly its five fields in order, exactly two types, a `verifyingContract`, all checked), DAI's `Permit`
  (`allowed: true` is no limit), and Permit2's `PermitSingle`, `PermitBatch`, `PermitTransferFrom` and
  `PermitBatchTransferFrom` (domain named "Permit2", no version, Permit2's canonical contract
  0x000000000022D473030F116dDEE9F6B43aC78BA3, exactly three types with their exact fields); a Soroban SEP-41
  `approve(from, spender, i128, u32)`, at the top or anywhere in an authorization tree (i128's max is no limit); NEAR
  NEP-178 `nft_approve` (amber). Typed data that calls itself Permit2 for another contract gets a red "This calls
  itself Permit2, but it isn’t for Permit2’s contract" line; any other typed data with a permit-like name or a
  `spender`/`operator` address field gets "This may be a permission to spend your tokens, in a form Journear can’t
  check". Permit2's witness transfers (`PermitWitnessTransferFrom`, `PermitBatchWitnessTransferFrom`: its domain, the
  four fields of the plain transfer, then one witness field) get the spend warning for each token and amount (a
  certain one-time spend) and stay unexplained (an amber "can't tell" line), since the witness is the app's own data.
- Token amounts: only a token on the pinned, reviewed list (`MAINNET_DEMO`: USDC and EURC on Base; XLM, USDC and EURC
  asset contracts on Stellar's public network) gets a symbol and decimals; any other amount is shown as signed, "in the
  token’s smallest units", of "tokens of contract 0x…". A contract's own `symbol()` and `decimals()` are its claim.
- Not covered: Uniswap-style routers, Permit2's `approve` transaction, NEAR `ft_transfer_call` receivers' later moves.
  A token transfer or approval authorized inside a Soroban contract creation is listed and warned like any other
  (D810, final review).
- After the second security review: an ERC-1155 `safeBatchTransferFrom` of up to five kinds lists each item and how
  many ("Item 7: 1,000"); `withdraw(uint256)` names its amount ("withdraw 1,000 (smallest units) from contract …");
  a generic call that sends the chain's coin says so in the headline ("…(deposit), sending it 0.1 ETH"). Amounts are
  grouped by thousands; item ids never are.
- NEP-413 (amended after the security review): the headline is neutral, "{App} wants you to sign a message for
  {recipient}", with the message and the recipient lines in view.
- Address impact: none.

- Date 2026-11-17 · Status: decided while building, **confirmed by the user 2026-11-17** · Built:
